To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the saccade kinematics of an E-saccades is determined by the center-of-gravity of activated SC cells and is independent of the microstimulation parameters.
the midbrain superiorcolliculus (SC), through its topographically organized population of neurons, generates a saccadic eye-movement vector that is independent of the stimulus intensity.
microstimulation of the SC activates a small population of cells, which sets off a large population response, and that the resulting E-saccades are kinematically similar to V-saccades.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the SC generates saccadic movements and how the network dynamics of the SC are affected by microstimulation.
the question of how the brain generates a rapid, goal-directed saccadic movement in response to a sensory stimulus.
the mechanisms that underly the generation of saccadic eye movements in the superior colliculus, and the way in which these mechanisms are reflected in the behavior of the animal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

microstimulation in a network of SC neurons with lateral synaptic interactions produces E-saccades with near-normal kinematic properties that are independent of the stimulus parameters, but with the exception of low stimulation intensities.
the SC motor map is not only a center-of-gravitation map, as suggested by the classic microstimulation results, but also a kinematic map.
both models are correct: the saccade trajectory is determined by a population center of gravity, but its kinematics arise from the population dynamics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SC population response, as evoked by microstimulation, can be used to generate an E-saccadic movement with near-normal kinematic properties.
the SC motor map encodes the desired saccadic trajectory, and that this information is robust to perturbations of the network.

the network model of the superior colliculus can reproduce microstimulation results, and thus is consistent with the idea that microstimulation produces a near-normal saccade by recruiting a large population of neurons through lateral synaptic interactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the network model of the superior colliculus is able to reproduce the kinematic properties of natural saccades, as well as the kinematic effects of microstimulation.
the microstimulation mechanism in the model is a parsimonious explanation for the kinematic properties of electrically evoked and visually evoked saccade trajectories.
the microstimulation results can be reproduced by the model without any assumptions about how the microstimulation affects the downstream feedback circuits.
